When the seller clearly states a firm price and negotiability, avoid making an initial offer significantly lower than your stated target price, as it may weaken your bargaining position.
When the seller confirms no damage but mentions replaced parts, avoid ignoring these details as they can be used to justify negotiating a lower price.
When the seller has acknowledged a minor issue with the item, you should leverage that flaw to justify a lower offer and strengthen your negotiation position.
When the seller offers a firm price with limited flexibility, you should introduce requests for additional value or extras to enhance the deal without lowering the price.
When the seller shows openness by asking for your price expectation, you should appeal to their empathy with financial constraints and personal need to encourage a specific counteroffer.

When the seller has made a clear counteroffer significantly above your initial price, avoid making a lowball offer that is only a small increase, as it can weaken your negotiation leverage and provoke rejection.
When the seller has made a high counteroffer and signaled willingness to negotiate, avoid prematurely stating your maximum price and closing off further negotiation.
